about.text:
The Regional Center for Social Science and Sustainable Development (RCSD) and the Center for Ethnic Studies and Development (CESD), Faculty of Social Sciences, Chiang Mai University, together with the National Centre for Borderlands Ethnic Studies in Southwest China and the School of Ethnology and Sociology at Yunnan University, are pleased to host the 3rd International Symposium on Coffee, Constructing the Coffee Landscape in the Southeast Asia Region: Commodity, Culture, and Knowledge in Transition, on 27–28 November 2026 at Chiang Mai University.

The symposium continues a series that began in Pu’er, Yunnan Province, China, with the Coffee Industry Global Value Chain Top Forum 2024, organised by the National Centre for Borderlands Ethnic Studies in Southwest China and the School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University. The series continued in Vietnam with Global and Sustainable Development: Coffee Industry Global Value Chain Top Forum 2025. This third meeting brings the conversation to northern Thailand.

Coffee in Southeast Asia has a long and uneven history. It began with colonial and missionary experiments and grew into a major export crop, from the plantation landscapes of Indonesia and Vietnam to state-led highland development in Thailand and Yunnan, and to the newer, small-scale production now emerging in Myanmar and Cambodia. Across these places, coffee is at once a global commodity, a crop shaped by local communities and ecologies, and an urban culture that is changing quickly. The symposium looks at how this landscape has been built, and how it continues to change: through the legacies of colonial and missionary history, the agrarian transitions of upland and lowland farming communities, and the pressures of climate change and the search for adaptation in agroforestry and farming systems.

Over two days, scholars, coffee growers and producers, development practitioners and entrepreneurs will exchange research and practice-based knowledge across six themes: coffee history; agriculture and agroforestry under climate change; coffee as commodity; coffee culture; agrarian transition; and knowledge production. Alongside paper sessions, panels and roundtables, the programme includes an exhibition and activities such as a public cupping.

In this workshop you'll eco-print fabric with coffee leaves and beans, blending your own shades into the cloth with your own hands.

Taste of Fermented reflects the idea of food as medicine, and of looking after yourself by understanding the craft of fermentation.

posts.title: Plenary Discussion II: Coffee, Land and Forest: Climate and Livelihoods of Upland Growers in Southeast Asia
posts.text:
Plenary Discussion II: Coffee, Land and Forest: Climate and Livelihoods of Upland Growers in Southeast Asia on Saturday, 28 November 2026 · 09:00–10:30 at Room 1 (Dhani Room), Faculty of Social Sciences, Chiang Mai University

Coffee has been promoted across the uplands of Southeast Asia as a crop that increases household income while maintaining forest cover. The income gains are well documented; the costs are recorded less often. This plenary presents three cases. In Manggarai, Indonesia, competing claims between customary cultivation and state-designated protected forest led to violence and a human rights investigation. In Dien Bien, Viet Nam, commercialization has shifted land, labour and investment away from subsistence production, raising cash income while increasing exposure to price and climate risk. In Thailand, most coffee is grown on land within forest zones without formal title, leaving growers' livelihoods dependent on insecure land tenure. Speakers will discuss what households lose in these transitions and what they need in order to farm securely under climate change.

posts.title: Roundtable II: Coffee Varieties and Soil Improvement for Adapting to Climate Change
posts.text:
Roundtable II: Coffee Varieties and Soil Improvement for Adapting to Climate Change on Friday, 27 November 2026 · 15:30–17:00 at Chamchuri Yard, Faculty of Social Sciences, Chiang Mai University

Coffee growers in the highlands of northern Thailand are already working with a changing climate: warmer seasons, irregular rainfall, and more pressure from pests and disease. This roundtable asks what research can do in practice.

Researchers from the Coffee Research and Development Center at Chiang Mai University's Faculty of Agriculture, which has studied coffee growing and processing for about thirty years, will discuss how varieties are selected and developed to cope with these conditions, and what growers should consider when choosing between them. A speaker from Maejo University will address soil improvement as the second part of adaptation, since soil health shapes both yield and a farm's resilience to climate stress.

The discussion asks which varieties and soil practices suit different altitudes and farming systems, how research findings reach growers, and what growers need in order to apply them. It connects to the symposium's themes of climate and livelihoods, and of whose knowledge counts in coffee.

posts.title: Roundtable I: New Generation Farmers and Women in Coffee Development
posts.text:
Roundtable I: New Generation Farmers and Women in Coffee Development, Friday, 27 November 2026, 12:30 am–1:30 pm, at Chamchuri Yard, Faculty of Social Sciences, Chiang Mai University. The roundtable will be conducted in Thai (TH-EN simultaneous translation provided).

A new generation of coffee farmers is returning to highland villages in northern Thailand. Many left for study or work in the city. They came back because coffee now offers a way to make a living at home, and for some, a high-value product that has won national recognition. Many of these new growers are young women.

This roundtable brings together three growers from highland communities in Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai to discuss why they returned, what they found when they did, and what they need to stay. They will also discuss who is recognized as the producer in the household and the community, and what changes when a new generation of farmers owns both the farm and the brand. The discussion links these experiences to the symposium's wider themes of land, climate, and whose knowledge counts in coffee.

Speakers:

posts.title: Keynote I: Thai Coffee in Transition: Structural Challenges and Emerging Possibilities
posts.text:
The 3rd International Symposium on Coffee is pleased to announce our keynote speaker, Dr. Fuadi Pitsuwan, Lecturer, Faculty of Political Science, Thammasat University, Vice President of the Specialty Coffee Association of Thailand (SCATH), and co-founder of Beanspire Coffee. His keynote address will be “Thai Coffee in Transition: Structural Challenges and Emerging Possibilities.” On Friday, 27 November 2026 · 09:45–10:30 · Room 1 (Dhani Room), Faculty of Social Sciences, Chiang Mai University

Throughout his academic career, Fuadi Pitsuwan was known for his expertise in international relations, and now he is a lecturer in International Relations at the Faculty of Political Science, Thammasat University. He received his bachelor’s degree from Georgetown University, his master’s degree from Harvard University, and his doctorate from the University of Oxford. His research has covered maritime security and the geopolitics of Southeast Asia, Indonesian foreign policy, and the relationship between linguistic identity and military alliances. He currently works on academic freedom and good governance in ASEAN and Myanmar. He is also a regular commentator on Thai policy towards Myanmar and the Thai-Myanmar border, and spoke at the plenary session on the border at the 5th International Conference on Burma/Myanmar Studies (ICBMS5) in August 2026.

Alongside his academic work, Dr. Fuadi has worked in Thai coffee for more than a decade as a coffee developer and exporter. Through Beanspire Coffee, he buys, processes, grades, and exports specialty coffee from highland farmers in northern Thailand, mainly in Chiang Rai, and has spent harvest seasons working with farmers on processing. As Vice President of the Specialty Coffee Association of Thailand, contributing to the development of Thai coffee.

Drawing on his experience across production, processing, and export, Dr. Fuadi will discuss the structural challenges facing Thai coffee today, from farm productivity and processing to quality, market access, and Thai coffee's place in regional and global markets. He will also consider the possibilities that are emerging as the industry changes.

posts.title: Plenary session 1: State of Coffee Production and Consumption in Southeast Asia and China
posts.text:
Plenary session 1 of the coffee symposium, "State of Coffee Production and Consumption in Southeast Asia and China" will be held on Friday, 27 November 2026 from 11:00 am. to 12:30 pm. in Room 1 (Dhani Room), Faculty of Social Sciences, Chiang Mai University

Coffee came to Indonesia, Thailand and Yunnan at different times and for different purposes, and each country’s coffee landscape reflects that history. Indonesia has the oldest export industry of the three. In Thailand, coffee was promoted as a state-supported highland development crop. Yunnan has shifted quickly from bulk supply to specialty production. All three now face uncertain open trade and fast-growing domestic consumption. This plenary brings together perspectives from research, sensory evaluation and social enterprise to review the current situation in each country, and to consider what it would take for the region to trade more directly within itself.

Speakers include Adi W. Taroepratjeka of 5758 Coffee Lab, Bandung, Indonesia; Fan Xu, coffee sensory assessor and consultant based in Guangzhou, China; and Lee Ayu Chuepa, founder of Akha Ama Coffee, Chiang Mai. They will discuss coffee as commodity, culture and knowledge in transition, covering the history and flavour mapping of Indonesian coffee, the changing value chains linking Yunnan to urban markets in China, and how purpose-driven specialty coffee can carry value back to producers.

blocks.title: Keynote I: Thai Coffee in Transition: Structural Challenges and Emerging Possibilities
blocks.about: This keynote examines the structural conditions that shape the Thai coffee sector. Import quotas and cross-border trade affect the price received at the farm gate. New requirements in export markets, including customs registration in China and due-diligence rules in the European Union, are making documentation a condition of market access. A significant share of highland production takes place on land for which growers hold no formal title. The keynote will address that these constraints are set at the level of trade and land policy, and cannot be resolved through improvements at farm level alone. It introduces two themes that run through the symposium: the position of coffee in agrarian transition, and the terms on which coffee from this region enters the global market.

papers.title: "Two Days Won't Do": A Told Landscape of Yunnan Coffee A Work-in-Progress Oral History and Visual Ethnography
papers.affiliation: Lecturer of Sociology in School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University
papers.abstract:
At the northern edge of the Southeast Asian upland coffee belt, Xiaowaozi Coffee Estate in Pu'er, Yunnan, shows how a coffee landscape is narrated and remembered. This paper presents a work-in-progress oral history and ethnographic film project based on ten days of fieldwork in August 2025 with the estate's founder, Mr. Liao.
Born in Hainan, where coffee was introduced by returned overseas Chinese from Southeast Asia, Mr. Liao was trained at the South China Institute of Tropical Agriculture and state-assigned to Yunnan. He worked tropical crops in Xishuangbanna before Nestlé's arrival brought him to Pu'er; after retirement, he bought a hillside hollow and became a roaster, café owner, and host. One life thus crosses three regimes—state assignment, contract farming, and family estate branding—condensing four decades of the region's coffee history.
The project's core observation is the told landscape: after decades of media coverage, Mr. Liao delivers a polished, pamphlet-like account with remarkable consistency. Through the slow presence he demands (“People come for two days and want to write about me; rushing through won't work”), the project traces how this public narrative yields to the personal—the technician's account, and finally the Hainanese layer: private memories of the homeland and family he left. On camera he rarely faces the lens; he addresses his photo albums. The estate emerges from what he looks at as much as from what he says.

papers.title: Paksong’s Coffee, Colonial Legacy to Indigenous Identity
papers.affiliation: World Wild Fund for Nature Laos (WWF-Laos)
papers.abstract:
Coffee arrived in many highland regions not as a gift but as an order. French colonial administrations in the early-to-mid 20th century saw the cool, high-altitude built on ancient volcanic terrain long inhabited by indigenous hill tribes and recognized only ideal terroir for a lucrative export crop. Plantations were carved from ancestral land through seizure and coercive policy, leaving local communities little say over their own ground.

Independence did not return land overnight, but it opened a door. Plantation structures fragmented over subsequent decades, and smallholder plots replaced centralized colonial estates. Indigenous families began working the same slopes their grandparents had once farmed under orders not fully or cleanly, given land disputes and market structures still favoring large exporters, but the direction was unmistakable from labor to stewardship.

What elevates this beyond economics is what happened to coffee’s meaning. For many hill tribe communities, it stopped being a foreign imposition and became a livelihood woven into cultural identity household processing techniques, village varietals, generational knowledge as pride rather than instruction. Cooperatives formed by indigenous growers began controlling not just farming but the story of the coffee itself, letting a family’s heritage travel from beans to cups worldwide a reversal of the crop’s anonymous, extractive origins.

The deepest shift is in the relationship to land. Where colonial farming prioritized short-term extraction, many growers now combine inherited ecological knowledge intercropping, shade management, water stewardship with coffee’s demands, treating the land as multigenerational responsibility rather than a resource to exhaust.

Coffee’s journey through these highlands mirrors colonial extraction giving way to self-determination a crop born of forced labor now representing continuity, independence, attraction for ecotourism and a family’s claim to the mountain they have always called home.
papers.keywords: Paksong · Indigenous · Coffee · Colonial

papers.title: The history of coffee, coffee-drinking culture, and social life in Aceh through Malay manuscript sources
papers.abstract: A cup of Acehnese coffee carries questions of history, sociability, and cultural knowledge that this study proposes to investigate through manuscripts. The study approaches coffee as a subject through which to explore the relationships between everyday consumption, social interaction, and the transmission of cultural knowledge. The study will use philological reading and historical contextualisation to examine Hikayat Gomtala Syah, Hikayat Kureh Pari, Tajul Muluk, and Hikayat Aceh for references to coffee and its consumption, with attention to textual provenance, dating, genre, and the circumstances in which particular accounts were produced. It asks how coffee and its consumption are represented in these sources, what social settings and relationships become visible through those representations, and how manuscript evidence can inform an understanding of Aceh’s living coffee culture. Particular attention will be given to the evidential limits of the sources and to the distinction between historical documentation and present-day interpretations of coffee traditions. The study will consider how locally situated accounts from Aceh can contribute to wider discussions of coffee as a commodity, a cultural practice, and a medium of knowledge exchange within Southeast Asia. Its intended contribution is to bring manuscript evidence into dialogue with the study of everyday social life and material culture, while identifying questions of continuity and change that require further investigation. The presentation will also incorporate selected Acehnese coffee samples and a traditional coffee cup as interpretive materials to support discussion of the relationships between written accounts, material objects, and contemporary coffee-drinking practices.
papers.keywords: Aceh · coffee history · manuscripts · coffee-drinking culture · social life

papers.title: Tasting the tradition: Coffee, Coorg, and the narratives of the ‘native’
papers.affiliation: Department of Sociology, School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Shiv Nadar Institute of Eminence, Deemed to be University, Delhi NCR
papers.abstract:
This paper explores how third-wave coffee makers, together with a set of partnering growers, reclaim the legacy of native culture by creating an affective economy centered on the sensorial characteristics of Coffee grown in native habitats. Since India’s coffee sector entered the free market in the mid-1990s, coffee has circulated through an expanding network of trading units, curing mills, and auction centers, transforming its movement and valuation. Based on my fieldwork across these institutions in the plantation villages of Coorg in Karnataka, South India, this paper articulates how coffee is represented and valued for its flavor and aroma, which simultaneously corresponds to the ways in which it is grown and cared for. 
Following global trends towards specialty and artisanal coffee, a few Kodavas, the local dominant community, have recently begun marketing their coffee as grown in ecologically diverse native habitats that produce premium-quality cups. This emerging value regime privileges flavor and aroma over conventional commercial coffee metrics such as size, color, moisture, and gravity. Growers, roasters, and Q-graders from Coorg work together to present ‘Coorg Coffee’ as a distinct sensorial object that both reflects its taste properties and represents the ‘native eco-system’ as the material condition in which coffee grows and develops its flavor profile. This native ecology is demonstrated as the reflection of Kodava cosmology, characterized by love for the land, preservation of tradition, and sacred forests, which becomes integral to coffee’s sensory value. 
Following anthropological literature on the production of quality in plantation economies (Besky 2020, Fischer 2022), this paper demonstrates that taste is coproduced through material, social, and discursive relations. Specialty coffee market, I argue, functions through an affective network among the grower, the coffee, and the consumer, navigated by the stories of Kodava life forms and the sustainable farming embedded in them.
papers.keywords: India · Specialty Coffee · Tradition · Native ecology

papers.title: Beyond the Instant Packet: Coffee Mix and Collective Deliberation in Karen Agrarian Landscapes
papers.abstract: In the forested agrarian landscapes of Southeast Myanmar, Indigenous Karen  communities maintain customary land governance (Kaw) and agroforestry livelihoods deeply intertwined with local natural resources. Yet, an intriguing cultural and material paradox exists across rural non-coffee-producing villages in this region: despite the absence of coffee bean farming, processing, or commercial teashop (laphet tye saing) culture, pre-packaged, industrial "3-in-1" coffee mix has become an indispensable technology of political and social life. Drawing on qualitative ethnographic fieldwork conducted between December 1 and December 17, 2025—comprising 24 semi-structured interviews and participant observations across village clusters—this study investigates the material, sensory, spatial, and gendered dimensions of instant coffee mix consumption. The findings reveal that coffee mix is deliberately withheld from daily routine labor and reserved exclusively as an "extraordinary" commodity for moments of formal assembly, guest reception, and community advancement meetings. Reaching for a factory-sealed sachet acts as a material boundary marker, re-spatializing the private domestic veranda (hter) into an autonomous political forum. The sensory properties of the beverage—its distinct aroma, concentrated sweetness, and rapid solubility—establish an affective social contract that fosters bodily alertness, calms interpersonal tension, and structures the temporal rhythms of consensus-building around land tenure and local security. Crucially, this public sphere of deliberation is underwritten by women’s affective and domestic labor, as women manage commodity reserves, control procurement, and prepare the beverage, serving as vital gatekeepers of local political space. By bridging political ecology, sensory anthropology, and material culture, this paper challenges production-centric biases in coffee geography. It demonstrates that agricultural commodities must be understood beyond zones of extraction, highlighting how Indigenous communities in conflict-affected borderlands strategically appropriate mass-manufactured consumer goods to sustain autonomous governance, collective solidarity, and political sovereignty.
papers.keywords: Coffee Mix · Karen Communities · Political Assembly

papers.title: An Anthropological Perspective on Vietnamese Coffee Culture
papers.affiliation: Researcher, Vietnam National Institute of Culture and Arts, Vietnam
papers.abstract:
Vietnam is not only famous for its rice cultivation, but is also one of the world's largest rice exporters. Its vast rice paddies stretch from north to south, and rice farming has become an important part of Vietnam's economic development. Father Alexander Vallet, a French priest, introduced the first coffee trees to Vietnam. However, the region's ecological environment and geographical conditions were unsuitable for coffee cultivation, so the coffee industry did not develop.

From 1925 to 1945, Vietnam gradually became a famous coffee-producing region. Due to its geographical location and climate, coffee is not only a popular beverage among Vietnamese people, but also a daily leisure activity and a cultural expression, a characteristic of Vietnamese culture. Whether enjoying a cup of fragrant hot coffee on a cold morning in Hanoi or sitting with friends on a rainy afternoon in Saigon, this has become a habit for many Vietnamese, forming a local cultural feature. What are the differences between the coffee cultures of Saigon and Hanoi? Hanoi and Saigon are the two largest cities in Vietnam and the centers of Vietnam's economic, political, cultural development and international exchange. The two cities, located approximately 1,730 kilometers apart, possess unique cultural characteristics, one of which is their coffee culture. Comparing the development of coffee consumption in Hanoi and Saigon, we can see significant differences in their social backgrounds and socio-ecological environments, resulting in their respective unique coffee cultures. Let's examine the following differences:

1. Coffee brewing methods, unique coffee flavors, and different names.

2. Places for enjoying coffee: at home, street-side coffee shops, large-scale coffee shops, and coffee chain stores.

3. Coffee drinkers: factors such as gender, age, and occupation all influence individual coffee drinking habits.

Through the above points, the author hopes to introduce Vietnamese coffee culture for discussion and academic exchange at the conference.
papers.keywords: Vietnamese coffee culture · anthropology of consumption · urban space · Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh · glocalization

papers.title: Designing Coffee Tourism: “Autonomous Design” and Indigenous Entrepreneurship in a Karen Community in Northern Thailand
papers.affiliation: Department of Tourism and Transnational Studies
papers.abstract:
Coffee has traditionally been regarded as a commodity that epitomizes the “North–South divide.” Specifically, critics have pointed to an unequal structure in which producers in the “South” (the Global South) grow coffee to meet demand in the “North” (developed nations), while the North dominates global coffee markets and captures the majority of the profits. In recent years, however, as coffee markets and cultures have matured, new initiatives have emerged in some producing regions that seek to independently manage the entire process, from cultivation and roasting to marketing and sales. Through this process of “sixth-sector industrialization” in coffee production, some coffee-related activities have also developed into new forms of “coffee tourism” by forging connections with the tourism sector.

   This presentation examines emerging trends in coffee tourism, focusing on Northern Thailand, where coffee markets and coffee culture have expanded rapidly since the 2010s. In ethnic Karen villages in Mae Hong Son Province, where the author has conducted fieldwork since the early 2000s, a recent phenomenon has emerged in which young people who previously worked in urban areas are returning to their home villages. These returnees are attempting to create autonomous spaces by combining traditional ways of life with the knowledge and experience they have acquired through urban life. As a case study, this presentation examines a coffee cultivation project launched by these returnees in 2023 through the perspectives of “autonomous design” (Escobar 2018) and “Indigenous entrepreneurship” (Eijdenberg et al. 2025), and explores its potential to foster alternative forms of economic and social development.
papers.keywords: coffee tourism · the Karen · Thailand · “autonomous design” · Indigenous entrepreneurship

papers.title: Brewing Mental Wellness: Craft Coffee Tourism as a Healing Experience, Ethical Commodification, and Destination Governance Opportunity in Vietnam
papers.abstract: Historically, health and wellness tourism has been dominated by spas and clinical settings, yet emerging evidence suggests that craft-based food tourism may offer meaningful mental wellness outcomes outside conventional therapeutic contexts. This case study examines how a Vietnamese coffee brand leverages farm-to-cup tourism to foster mindfulness, sensory awareness, and intellectual wellbeing among visitors. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with the founder and participant observation at the farm's roastery and café, the study explores the intersection of food tourism and individual wellbeing. Findings reveal that the multisensory experience of observing coffee beans, engaging with varying roasting profiles, and participating in cupping (tasting) rituals cultivates a mindfulness practice of slowing down and sensory attunement. This experience counteracts the negative effects of consumerism on tourists' intellectual wellbeing by fostering pride and knowledge of product provenance, while also serving as a partial healing mechanism outside clinical settings (Zheng et al., 2025). From a supply-side perspective, the case highlights significant governance challenges, including the owner's commitment to maintaining a quality, authentic, non-scaled product at the expense of digital marketing, and the absence of state acknowledgment of "wellness food tourism." These dynamics illuminate broader issues of inequality and care commodification: while wealthy international tourists constitute the target market, local community members and poorer travelers are largely excluded. Moreover, local tourism boards lack the coordination necessary to integrate wellness tourism and craft producers into broader destination strategies. The study concludes by offering governance recommendations for destination managers to develop "wellness routes"—networks connecting diverse producers to different traveler segments—to ensure that the mental health benefits of craft tourism are sustained and equitably distributed. This case contributes to emerging discourse on alternative wellness tourism models and their potential for inclusive, community-oriented mental health promotion.
papers.keywords: wellness tourism · food tourism · mental health · Vietnam · craft coffee

papers.title: Integrating Agriculture and Tourism in Yunnan Coffee Estates Operating Models of Gongjiang and Dakaihe Meizi Coffee Estates in Yunnan
papers.abstract: Coffee estates in Yunnan increasingly combine production with visitor services, creating a managerial challenge of connecting agriculture, cultural expression, and tourism within a coherent operating model. This paper compares Gongjiang Coffee Estate in Baoshan and Dakaihe Meizi Coffee Estate in Pu’er. An exploratory qualitative case study brings together the author’s interview with the proprietor of Gongjiang Coffee Estate and published journalistic, institutional, and fieldwork reports, with limited descriptive support from a survey conducted mainly at Dakaihe. Resource orchestration and experience co-creation guide comparison of production resources, service combinations, knowledge interpretation, market connections, and operating constraints. The cases suggest two overlapping orientations. Gongjiang’s reported agricultural setting and interview discussion foreground an agricultural foundation for cultural and visitor development. Dakaihe Meizi’s documented trajectory connects processing expertise and the proprietor’s narrative with cafés, organized production visits, and accommodation. Their common managerial task is to make coffee production accessible and meaningful through coordinated spaces, activities, and explanation. The comparison suggests that the coherence of these connections matters more analytically than the number of services offered. It also identifies agricultural seasonality and the organization of interpretation as conditions shaping the delivery of experiences. By examining how productive resources acquire cultural and visitor-facing uses, the paper offers a focused management perspective on changing coffee landscapes. The findings describe operating arrangements and development priorities rather than establish comparative profitability or causal effects.
papers.keywords: coffee estates · agritourism · operating models · resource orchestration · knowledge interpretation

papers.title: Resilience of Coffee Communities: A hidden story of ethnic communities from Chiang Mai Province, Thailand
papers.abstract:
Climate change threatens to global coffee production, particularly for Arabica coffee, which is sensitive to temperature and rainfall variations. While existing research heavily focuses on crop-level resilience or regions in Latin America and Africa regions, there remains a critical knowledge gap regarding Southeast Asian smallholder coffee producers, specifically ethnic minority from the Northern Thailand. This study investigates the community resilience approach and climate adaptation strategies by exploring the backgrounds and socio-ecological support systems of ethnic communities in rapidly growing coffee destinations of Chiang Mai Province, Thailand. Moreover, it examines the intersectionality of local agricultural practices, traditional ecological knowledge, institutional support systems and multi-scalar power structures. The findings of this study spotlight on ‟how upland hilltribe communities navigate state conservation laws, land rights struggles, and market pressures” while transitioning from historical swidden agriculture to sustainable agroforestry and specialty coffee production. 
By using a political ecology approach, it investigates the resilience of coffee-producing villages where ethnic minorities maintain unique cultures and identity. The study highlights ecological vulnerability and socio-political marginalization providing multi-dimensional views of ethnic coffee communities. Employing qualitative methods, including observation and in-depth interviews, it examines land-use practices, agricultural management, and the impacts of conservation laws and traditional customs. 
The research captures local knowledge and perceptions of climate change, resilience, and adaptation strategies through observation and interviews with farmers, community members, and support institutions. By analyzing the social and environmental conditions of these communities, the study addresses opportunities and challenges in implementing adaptation measures to strengthen resilience against the consequences of climate change. Ultimately, this study aims to inform policymakers, private sectors, and agricultural stakeholders on enhancing the adaptive capacity, socio-economic stability, and environmental sustainability of vulnerable coffee-farming communities in Thailand and beyond.
papers.keywords: Adaptation Measures · Coffee · Community Resilience · Climate Change · Political Ecology

papers.title: Dynamics of Coffee Consumption and the Development of Coffee Shops in Kendari, Southeast Sulawesi, Indonesia
papers.abstract:
Consuming coffee at coffee shops has become a growing lifestyle in Kendari, the capital city of Southeast Sulawesi Province, Indonesia. Coffee consumption at coffee shops is not merely drinking or enjoying coffee, but coffee shops serve as public spaces where consumers gather and engage in various activities. Coffee consumption patterns are not only determined by consumer demographics, such as age and gender, but also by the development of coffee processing technology. Therefore, besides long-established traditional coffee shops, various new formats have emerged, such as modern coffee shops, street-side coffee stalls, and mobile coffee vendors.
Based on the background above, this paper will describe the dynamics of coffee consumption and the development of coffee shops in Kendari. The research adopts cultural anthropology perspectives and uses ethnographic methods with two main elements: participant observation and in-depth interviews. Participant observation is conducted at several coffee shops in Kendari, while in-depth interviews are conducted with both consumers and coffee shop owners or managers.
The research findings show that coffee shops in Kendari can be categorized into two general types: traditional and modern. Traditional coffee shops serve coffee using simple and traditional methods: brewing coffee grounds with hot water and filtering the mixture using a cloth filter. Meanwhile, modern coffee shops serve coffee using modern machines, resulting in various coffee types with contemporary names, such as espresso, caffè latte, or cappuccino. Based on demographic categories, the consumers of traditional coffee shops are mostly men above 40 years old, whereas consumers of modern coffee shops are mostly young people, both men and women, under 40 years old. In fact, coffee culture in Kendari has developed with a long-standing history rooted in the existence of traditional coffee shops, and later it underwent cultural reconstruction and reproduction with the emergence of modern coffee shops.
papers.keywords: coffee consumption · coffee shops · Kendari · cultural reproduction

papers.title: Coffee Raves in Thailand: Coffee and the Making of Leisure
papers.affiliation: Graduate School of Asian and African Area Studies, Kyoto University
papers.abstract:
In recent years, coffee raves, daytime events combining coffee, music, and dancing, have attracted attention across Southeast Asia. Often presented as healthier alternatives to conventional nightlife, these events offer opportunities for music and social interaction without necessarily involving alcohol. However, coffee raves differ in their use of coffee, venues, and approaches to leisure.
This paper examines how event organizers and venue operators envision different forms of leisure and assign roles to coffee in realizing them. Based on interviews and participant observation conducted in Chiang Mai and Bangkok, Thailand, between August and September 2026, the study compares three coffee rave events held at two cafés and one bar.
The findings reveal that the roles assigned to coffee vary according to the forms of leisure that organizers and venue operators seek to create. At Café A, coffee provides an option for those who wish to enjoy music and social interaction without consuming alcohol. At Café B, the organizer emphasizes dancing, music, and a natural environment rather than coffee itself, envisioning a relaxed and health-conscious party. At Bar C, coffee serves as an entry point to daytime parties that bring together people with different attitudes toward drinking and health. The subsequent introduction of alcoholic beverages at Bar C also demonstrates how coffee's role can be adjusted through event operations.
These cases suggest that coffee's role in coffee raves is not determined solely by the beverage or the event's name. Instead, it is shaped and adjusted in relation to the forms of leisure envisioned by organizers and venue operators. By examining these relationships, this study highlights how coffee is incorporated into the organization of leisure activities, offering a perspective on coffee culture that extends beyond beverage consumption.
papers.keywords: Coffee culture · Chiang Mai · cafés · sociality · coffee consumption

papers.title: From Ritual Hospitality to Digital Distinction: Revaluing Coffee in Urban Indonesia
papers.abstract:
**From Ritual Hospitality to Digital Distinction: Revaluing Coffee in Urban Indonesia**

Coffee in Indonesia is commonly described either as an agricultural commodity or as a rapidly expanding urban lifestyle. This paper argues that its contemporary social significance is better understood as a process of **revaluation**, through which inherited meanings of hospitality, ritual, locality, and sociality are selectively translated into new forms of commercial, symbolic, and digital value. Drawing on qualitative field research in Jakarta, Yogyakarta, and Makassar, including observations in traditional and modern coffee spaces and semi-structured interviews with fifteen consumers and five coffee-industry practitioners, the study compares how coffee acquires different meanings across three urban contexts.

The findings identify four interrelated modes of social valuation: religious and ritual hospitality, social relationship, life-cycle commemoration, and social distinction. In Makassar, coffee remains embedded in post-Ramadan religious gatherings while regional origins such as Toraja and Kalosi are simultaneously reformulated as markers of authenticity and local identity in modern cafés. In Yogyakarta, vernacular coffee practices coexist with specialty cafés, coffee catering, and creative communities, while in Jakarta coffee shops increasingly operate as spaces of professional networking, lifestyle performance, and status differentiation. Across the three cities, cafés, branding practices, origin narratives, visual aesthetics, and social media transform coffee from a beverage into a medium for constructing identity and distinction.

Rather than representing a linear shift from tradition to modernity, these processes demonstrate how local meanings are repeatedly reworked through commodity circulation and digital representation. The paper proposes the notion of **urban coffee landscapes as infrastructures of valuation**, where place, ritual, taste, class, and mediated visibility intersect. It contributes to understanding how Southeast Asian coffee cultures are being transformed not through the disappearance of local traditions, but through their selective incorporation into contemporary markets and regimes of distinction.
papers.keywords: Keywords: coffee landscape · social valuation · urban coffee culture · distinction · commodity

papers.title: Tracing Coffee’s Place in Ethnobotanical Practice: case study from Mae Klang Luang Karen Village, Chiang Mai
papers.abstract: Despite its non-native origins, coffee has established a cultivated relationship with highland ethnic groups in northern Thailand. In Chiang Mai province, the Karen highland ethnic group is widely recognized for their coffee-crafting practices. This paper applies an ethnobotanical lens and discussion to explore how coffee as both a plant and an economic product continuously reshapes social and cultural dynamics in Mae Klang Luang Karen Village. Four decades after its introduction as a substitute to opium through King Rama IX’s Royal Project, coffee has evolved from an unfamiliar cash crop into the village’s signature. Through institutional sharing knowledge from the Royal Project and other institutions, Mae Klang Luang has transformed coffee into a cultural tradition and tourism experience by serving coffee as a welcome drink. This study employs qualitative fieldwork including in-depth and semi-structured interviews as well as participant’s observation. The study finds a threefold impact: ecologically, a shade-grown coffee practice enhances forest conservation, economically, coffee shops serve as the hub for selling local products such as local fruits and vegetables and handicrafts such as hand-woven clothes and bags, and culturally, nature trail tourism led by local Karen guides turn coffee origin stories into immersive ethnobotanical learning for tourists. These findings demonstrate how a single plant species can reshape a community’s development path, highlighting the role of ethnobotanical traditions in contemporary highland livelihoods.
papers.keywords: Ethnobotany · Coffee culture · Karen ethnic group

papers.title: The Changing Trajectory of Community-Based Coffee Farming and Processing in Barangay Talbak, Doña Remedios Trinidad, Bulacan, Philippines
papers.abstract: This study explores the evolving landscape of community-based coffee farming and processing in Barangay Talbak, located in Doña Remedios Trinidad, Bulacan, Philippines. The history of coffee farming in this community is linked to the migration of families from Cavite, a region in the southern Philippines, during the 1960s and 1970s. These settlers moved to Talbak in search of agricultural land and brought with them the knowledge and practices associated with coffee cultivation. Over time, coffee farming has become an integral part of the community's agricultural livelihood and local knowledge. This qualitative study aims to understand how the coffee landscape has evolved by examining the experiences and perspectives of coffee farmers and other key community members. Using a historical-contextual approach, the study will conduct semi-structured interviews to explore the development of coffee farming and processing. It will investigate the factors that have influenced its changing trajectory, as well as the responses and adaptations of local farmers. The interviews will be analyzed thematically to identify patterns related to production, processing, livelihoods, markets, environmental conditions, agricultural knowledge, and other factors shaping the community’s coffee landscape. By documenting the experiences and perspectives of coffee-growing communities in Talbak, this study offers a localized perspective on broader discussions of coffee landscapes in Southeast Asia. It specifically addresses issues of migration, knowledge, livelihoods, and the evolving nature of community-based coffee production.
papers.keywords: coffee farming · coffee landscapes · coffee processing · migration · community-based agriculture

papers.title: Seeing Sustainability: A Participatory Visual Study of Coffee Farmers’ Knowledge, Negotiation, and Aspirations
papers.abstract: This paper examines how smallholder coffee farmers in Nan Province, Thailand, define, enact, and transmit sustainability through their everyday practices. Drawing on agroecology (Altieri, 2004; Gliessman, 2018) and Dobson's (2007) relational theory of environmental citizenship, the paper argues that farmers are not passive recipients of expert knowledge but active producers, interpreters, and transmitters of it. Using participatory visual methods, including Photovoice, semi-structured interviews, and a focus group, seven coffee farmers in Nan documented and discussed their own definitions of sustainability, the local knowledge underpinning their practices, the challenges they face, and their aspirations for their land and communities. Findings show that farmers hold relational, holistic definitions of sustainability centered on care, intergenerational responsibility, and livelihood security, definitions that routinely exceed narrow, metric-driven institutional framings. Farmers also generate adaptive agroecological knowledge through experience and peer exchange, at times departing from official agricultural guidance to better suit local conditions. Despite significant structural and social challenges, including isolation from conventional farming neighbors and limited market access, farmers sustain strong aspirations for their land and communities, and many actively position themselves as informal educators, mentoring younger farmers and partnering with local schools. The paper concludes that coffee farmers in Nan are already enacting agroecology and environmental citizenship in practice and connects this to a broader concern with epistemic justice (Fricker, 2007) in agricultural knowledge systems, arguing that recognizing farmers as legitimate knowledge-holders is a necessary step toward sustainability education and policy that works with, rather than against, local realities.
papers.keywords: Agroecology · Environmental Citizenship · Participatory Visual Methods · Coffee Farming · Thailand

papers.title: Sourcing Coffee Beans, Taking Root, and Building Together: The Practices and Contributions of the “New Yunnanese” in Qinglan County’s Coffee Industry from a Brokerage Perspective
papers.affiliation: Professor of Sociology, School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University, Doctoral Student of Sociology, School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University
papers.abstract:
In recent years, Yunnan’s coffee industry has gradually expanded beyond cultivation and primary processing into specialty coffee production, branding, and other forms of coffee-related tourism and extended stays. The development of the industry has become increasingly intertwined with population mobility, local tourism, and community development. However, the arrival of external resources does not necessarily lead to deeper social integration into local communities, nor does industrial growth automatically make newcomers active participants in local development. Against this backdrop, this article asks: How do external actors, particularly the “New Yunnanese” seize the opportunities created by the development of the coffee industry to move from entering a locality to becoming intermediaries and active participants in industrial and community development? How does this transformation take place? How are relationships established between these actors and local industries, producers, and other social actors? In turn, how does the local industry shape their sense of identity and their relationships with the locality?

This study is situated in a coffee-producing county in southwestern China, referred to here by the pseudonym “Qinglan County”. The local coffee industry is closely intertwined with external market connections, the mobility of people and expertise, and emerging forms of community development, providing a concrete setting in which to examine how newcomers participate in local development. Lin Chuan (a pseudonym) serves as the focal case. Drawing on preliminary fieldwork, interviews, and relevant documentary materials, this study traces Lin’s experiences of entering the locality, becoming involved in the coffee industry, and building social relationships. Accounts from other actors involved in the local industry are also examined to assess Lin’s practices of brokering connections and their practical effects.

Drawing on Lin Chuan’s experiences, this study first examines how the coffee industry creates opportunities for newcomers to enter local society and how Lin gradually establishes relationships with local producers and other participants through production collaborations, technical exchanges, and industry-related activities. It then analyzes how Lin connects specialized knowledge with local production, local producers with external markets, and industrial activities with community life, engaging in practices of knowledge translation, information exchange, relationship coordination, and collaborative organization. The analysis thus extends beyond the introduction of external resources by newcomers to consider how the locality, in turn, shapes newcomers themselves, examining how opportunities arising from industrial development, local social relationships, and sustained participation influence Lin’s role positioning and sense of local identity. This study adopts the concept of the “ferryman” as an analytical perspective for understanding how external actors establish connections across different groups of actors and resource systems. The term “New Yunnanese”, by contrast, refers to the identity transformation that develops through sustained participation and relational interactions. The two concepts are not equivalent: the capacity to broker connections is not an inherent attribute of newcomers, nor does identity transformation necessarily indicate deep integration into local society. Both must be assessed in relation to concrete practices, responses from other actors, and changes in social relationships.

This study argues that the significance of external actors’ participation in local development lies not only in their introduction of external resources, but also in their ability to transform knowledge, market access, and opportunities for collaboration into conditions for development that local communities can participate in and sustain through ongoing social connections. The relationship between newcomers and the locality is not simply one of external resources being introduced and locally received; rather, both are mutually shaped through industrial practices and social interactions. Adopting the “ferryman” perspective, this study seeks to bring together discussions of specialty industry development, population mobility, and local integration, illuminating the processes through which newcomers move from entering a locality to participating in its development, as well as the conditions and limits of this transition. The study contributes to a deeper understanding of the social effects of Yunnan’s coffee industry. It also offers an empirical point of reference for examining the relationships among specialty industry development, the integration of newcomers with specialized expertise, and community development in other settings, while providing insights for comparative research on these issues across different regions of China and in Southeast Asian societies.
papers.keywords: Specialty Coffee Industry · New Yunnanese · Broker · Local Embeddedness · Collaborative Place-making

papers.title: Beyond Evasion: Coffee, Agrarian Capitalism, and State Engagement in an Akha Community of Northern Thailand
papers.affiliation: Faculty of Social Sciences, Chiang Mai University
papers.abstract:
This research explores the agrarian transition and capitalization process within Mae Chan Tai, an Akha ethnic village in northern Thailand, following the introduction of commercial coffee farming. The study aims to address the central research question ‘How does the transition to agrarian capitalism reshape an ethnic community’s relations with the state and the social relations within the community?’ To answer this, the research expands upon James C. Scott’s concept of Zomia by employing Tania Murray Li’s concepts of Rendering Technical from Govermentality, alongside Henry Bernstein’s Agrarian Differentiation Theory. Data were collected using a qualitative approach comprising in-depth interviews and field observations.
The findings reveal three significant shifts. First, agricultural commercialization supported by the Royal Project and external development organizations such as GIAPSA (NPO) has expanded the community's interactions with the state and external markets, with coffee serving as an economic intermediary. Rather than indicating a complete transition from state evasion to state acceptance, this process reflects the emergence of new economic relationships and opportunities for villagers to develop their own businesses. Second, capitalist incorporation has introduced new market-oriented relationships alongside existing forms of mutual dependence and collective cooperation. The emergence of 15 coffee brands among 43 households reflects the expansion of entrepreneurship and economic competition, while community-based economic cooperation continues to exist. Finally, the economic success of the local coffee industry has attracted the younger generation back to the village, running counter to the common trend of rural-to-urban migration. This economic strength not only rebuilds the community's demographic future but may also open up space for studying bargaining power with the state in other dimensions. This study demonstrates that capitalist incorporation has generated new economic and social relationships that coexist with existing community relations, contributing to increasingly complex interactions among the community, the state, and the market.
papers.keywords: Agrarian Capitalism · State Engagement · Zomia · Akha · Coffee

papers.title: Coffee and Everyday World-making Among Akha in Northern Thailand: Land History and Place Attachment at Doi Tung
papers.abstract:
Where Akha households held usable land and a say over its use, they invested in staying. Where state classification removed land and ignored customary rules, households turned to wage labour, stopped seeing themselves as forest guardians, and could no longer meet some ritual obligations. Thai highland policy has been top-down and has defined development without Akha participation. At Doi Tung, coffee moved from a substitution crop to a branded commodity. This paper builds an exploratory framework from the perspectives of historical political ecology to study examine how the land territorialization and change of the livelihoods are shaping the cultural recognition of Akha identity incorporating cultural ecosystem services (CES). attachment of Akha coffee growers at Doi Tung, northern Thailand. Taking Akha tea plantation in Yunnan Province of China as a starting point this paper analyses sense of place amidst the collision between sustainable development in Akhazang and land use policy in northern Thailand. This exploratory article brings historical political ecology into dialogue with cultural exist services research on place, memory and daily practice, rituals, commercial coffee production in Doi Tung’s shade growing Arabic coffee landscape. Drawing on socially engaged art Eat proposes participatory design that combines participate, land, walking, interviews, mapping and drawing with collaborative design workshop adapted from Khirfan’s combined charrette. The design aims at residents to compare how they use and remember the same places and to decide together how their relationships with the ancestors, tree deities, the wider nature are represented in daily practice of coffee cultivation.
Keywords: Akha, Doi Tung, coffee landscapes, place attachment, cultural ecosystem services
papers.keywords: Coffee · Akha · world-making · knowledge production · social reproduction

papers.title: Scaling Quality, Unevenly: Specialty Coffee and Agrarian Change in the Cordillera Highlands of the Philippines
papers.abstract:
This paper examines how specialty coffee standards reorganize agrarian relations among Indigenous Ibaloi and Kankana-ey farmers in Atok, Benguet, and why these changes remain uneven. Drawing on ten months of multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork (2024–2026) centered on nine coffee-farming households, interviews with downstream coffee actors, and historical materials, I situate contemporary specialty production within an Indigenous coffee world shaped by inherited land, locally embedded labor, and longstanding trading relationships. Earlier assessments by Baguio coffee traders and government-linked agricultural training already informed how farmers processed and sold coffee. Contemporary specialty markets extend these evaluative practices through cupping and more closely specified processing standards.
Drawing on political ecology and Anna Tsing's concept of nonscalability, I show how quality requirements enter cultivation and postharvest work under conditions that cannot be standardized uniformly. Farmers recalibrate judgments of ripeness and drying while negotiating limited land and uneven access to processing infrastructure. A coffee's classification also depends partly on whether buyers can verify its processing history; comparable care or cupping scores do not necessarily yield the same market recognition. Following Thiers's account of changing disciplinary logics, I understand specialty coffee as a mutation of earlier market disciplines.
I develop disciplined aspiration to describe how farmers pursue dependable buyers and recognition through standards that simultaneously reorganize their work. Specialty, premium, and commercial coffee continue to circulate within the same ili (village), revealing how shared standards encounter different agrarian conditions. The paper contributes to debates on agrarian change and the politics of value in Southeast Asian coffee production.
papers.keywords: Specialty coffee · coffee quality · Indigenous farmers · agrarian change · value

blocks.title: Plenary Discussion II: Coffee, Land and Forest: Climate and Livelihoods of Upland Growers in Southeast Asia: Cases from Indonesia, Viet Nam, and Thailand
blocks.about: Coffee has been promoted across the uplands of the region as a crop that increases household income while maintaining forest cover. The income gains are documented. The associated costs are less often recorded. This plenary presents four cases. In Manggarai, Indonesia, competing claims between customary cultivation and state-designated protected forest led to violence and a human rights investigation. In Dien Bien, Viet Nam, commercialisation has shifted land, labour and investment away from subsistence production, increasing cash income while raising exposure to price and climate risk. In Thailand, most of coffee cultivate land within a forest zone without formal documentation, the livelihood that may has a dilemma of land tenure. Speakers will discuss what households lose in these transitions and what is required for them to farm securely.

papers.title: Localized globalization: The Heritagization and Decolonization of Vietnamese Coffee Culture
papers.affiliation: School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University
papers.abstract: For a long time, Vietnamese coffee culture, as a colonial legacy, has been widely embraced by the Vietnamese people and deeply embedded in their everyday life, giving rise to a distinctively Vietnamese style of phin drip-filter coffee. In recent years, however, amid the transformation of Vietnam’s coffee industry, both the Vietnamese government and domestic coffee enterprises have been actively promoting the re-creation of indigenous coffee culture. Notably, in 2025, the inscription of the Knowledge of Coffee Cultivation and Processing in Đắk Lắk Province onto Vietnam’s National List of Intangible Cultural Heritage represents an outcome of the state’s drive toward the heritagization of coffee culture. Meanwhile, Vietnamese coffee enterprises, most notably Trung Nguyên Coffee, have been reshaping the image and positioning of Vietnamese coffee in both domestic and international markets by establishing the “Coffee Dao” (the Way of Coffee) and founding coffee museums. This top-down heritagization of Vietnamese coffee culture and the concomitant construction of “localized globalization” demonstrate the translation and re-creation of Vietnamese coffee culture against the backdrop of global connectivity, while simultaneously constituting a decolonizing engagement with colonial heritage.

papers.title: Body, Nature, and the Gaze: A Study on the Cheat code forviews and Cultural Mechanisms of China's influencer Cafes
papers.affiliation: School of Law and Politics, Yunnan University of Finance and Economics
papers.abstract:
In recent years, various influencer Cafés that combine sensory experiences such as taste and sight have emerged in China, becoming a new form of tourism in the context of cultural and tourism integration. This study focuses on several
popular and highly representative influencer Cafes in China, conducting an in-depth analysis to argue that visiting these cafés has become a cultural phenomenon reflecting nature, visual aesthetics, and bodily experience within tourism. Judging from
current forms—such as waterfall cafés and cave cafés—coffee consumption is deeply integrated with tourism experiences, involving observation, physical sensations, and people's exploration and aspirations toward nature. In today’s tourism consumption, gaze theory and embodiment theory alone are insufficient to fully explain the underlying cultural and social meanings and the mechanisms behind this phenomenon. Drawing on cultural sociology, this study attempts to analyze the cultural mechanisms emerging from the fusion of symbolic consumption and bodily experience, thereby proposing a new theoretical framework for understanding tourism experiences.

papers.title: When the Highlands Move: Coffee, Ethnicity, and Regional Politics of Belonging in Thailand
papers.abstract: This article examines how coffee production acquires different meanings beyond Thailand’s northern highlands into new settings. It compares the established Arabica coffee economy associated with Akha entrepreneurship in Chiang Rai with an emerging Robusta initiative among Tai Dam producers in Loei Province. Rather than treating these cases as equivalent, the article approaches them as distinct trajectories shaped by institutional histories, market conditions, and relationships between ethnicity and economic opportunity. The analysis draws on scholarship on highland crop replacement and ethnicized coffee commerce, alongside ten semi-structured interviews with Tai Dam coffee producers conducted on 20 October 2026. All ten interviewees reported receiving provincial funding to begin coffee production, and all described their plantations as being at an early stage. Only one explicitly identified Tai Dam identity as important to coffee branding; the other nine did not identify ethnicity as a branding priority. This finding does not indicate that ethnic identity is unimportant elsewhere. Drawing on Benedict Anderson’s concept of imagined communities and Pierre Bourdieu’s concepts of habitus and symbolic capital, the article argues that the commercial use of ethnic identity depends on institutional and market context. The movement of coffee, therefore, does not necessarily entail the movement of ethnic identity into the marketplace.
papers.keywords: Isan · Tai Dam · Akha

papers.title: Producing the “Sustainable” Coffee Landscape: Political Ecology, Value Chains, and Smallholder Livelihoods in the Gayo Highlands of Aceh, Indonesia
papers.abstract: Southeast Asia's coffee landscapes are being changed by the combination of global specialty-coffee markets, sustainability interventions, climate change, and evolving rural governance. This research investigates these processes in the Gayo Highlands of Aceh, Indonesia, where smallholder Arabica production is both rooted in global value chains and contested local landscapes of land, forest, and livelihoods. Using political ecology and a critical global value chain (GVC) perspective, the paper investigates how sustainability interventions and global coffee markets reshape smallholder producers' access to land, resources, knowledge, and value, and what the implications are for livelihood and environmental justice. Existing research has demonstrated that coffee upgrading and sustainability programs can create new market opportunities, but they can also perpetuate local inequalities by limiting access to money, markets, institutions, and decision-making. Research on Indonesian coffee shows that the benefits of "relationship coffee" and value-chain upgrading are frequently reaped by locally powerful players, but sustainability programs may have limited compatibility with current livelihoods. However, little attention has been paid to how environmental governance, gendered interactions, climate adaptation, and value-chain reconfiguration intersect geographically within the same coffee landscape. The study's methodology is a qualitative, multi-scalar approach that includes semi-structured interviews with farmers, cooperatives, traders, government and development actors, participant observation, life histories, and analysis of coffee certification, land-use, and policy papers. By linking everyday livelihood practices to larger commodity governance processes, the paper contends that "sustainable coffee" should be viewed as a contested political process in which value, environmental responsibility, and resource access are negotiated. It thus combines studies on political ecology, agrarian change, and GVCs to demonstrate how sustainability is produced and unevenly distributed across the Gayo coffee landscape.
papers.keywords: Political Ecology · Coffee Landscapes · Global Value Chains · Smallholder Livelihoods · Environmental Justice

papers.title: Between Field and Market: Middlemen as Local Market Regulators, Corporate Connectors, and EUDR Adapters in Vietnam’s Coffee Chain
papers.affiliation: Phuoc Son Agricultural Trading Ltd. Company
papers.abstract: Local coffee traders connect smallholder farmers to large buying companies, but their significance extends beyond commodity purchasing. This paper examines middlemen in Vietnam’s Central Highlands as de facto local market regulators and corporate connectors whose purchasing, information, informal finance, and traceability functions shape farmers’ access to markets. Drawing on sector literature, Vietnamese press reports, and the author’s practice-based observations within a coffee trading and 4C-certification program in Lam Dong Province, it develops the concept of trader dependency: situations in which access to production credit, inputs, market information, and sales channels becomes concentrated within a durable trader relationship. These relationships provide organizational reach, liquidity, and market access that many sustainability programs lack, but they can also constrain farmers’ choices and create risks of exclusion. Land-tenure insecurity sharpens the condition: households without documented rights find formal finance and sustainability programs harder to reach, and the trader’s bundle of services fills the resulting gap. Their protective function can also be reversed. Recurrent insolvencies of buying agents holding farmers’ consigned coffee show how sharp price movements and defaults on either side can turn established relationships into channels of loss and erode trust. This fragility matters because sustainability interventions operate through existing intermediary networks rather than independently of them, a dynamic made particularly visible by traders’ operational adaptation to the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR). The central policy challenge is therefore not disintermediation but governance: designing institutions capable of aligning intermediary incentives with inclusive and environmentally sustainable rural development and of protecting the trust on which the middleman’s market-regulating, connective, and compliance functions all depend.
papers.keywords: Middlemen · Coffee Certification · Sustainability · Trader dependency · EUDR

papers.title: Brewing inequality in Flores Coffee: Entrepreneurial Mediation, Logistics, and Unequal Value Chains
papers.abstract: This paper examines how coffee farmers in Flores, Indonesia, experience participation in specialty and sustainability-oriented markets. It asks how logistics, harvest timing, buyer and certification requirements shape farmers’ ability to capture value and exercise agency within the coffee value chain. The study draws on qualitative interviews with ten coffee farmers in Flores, complemented by the author’s reflexive account as a coffee entrepreneur and intermediary in the region. The analysis focuses on three connected issues: inter-island transport and freight costs; constraints associated with a concentrated annual harvest; and certification and traceability requirements that privilege documented evidence. It considers how these conditions shape farmers’ bargaining room, the distribution of costs and risks, and the representation of local production practices to distant buyers. The analysis suggests that access to specialty markets can create opportunities while leaving farmers exposed to logistical, temporal, and compliance burdens shaped beyond the place of production. By foregrounding farmers’ accounts and linking them to the wider organization of the coffee trade, the paper offers a place-based perspective on coffee as a commodity. It argues for greater transparency in the allocation of logistics and compliance costs and for recognition of producer-defined priorities in market relationships.
papers.keywords: Flores coffee · coffee value chains · smallholder farmers · market access · certification

papers.title: Volatility, Financialization, and the Global Value Chain Imbalance in the World Coffee Market
papers.affiliation: Distinguished Researcher, National Centre for Borderlands Ethnic Studies in Southwest China at Yunnan University
papers.abstract: Green coffee is among the most important agricultural commodities in world trade, and among the most volatile. This paper examines four propositions about that volatility: that its first-order roots lie in the biological-agronomic cycle of a perennial tree crop compounded by climate shocks; that financialization over the past five decades has amplified the resulting swings; that demand is strongly price-rigid, so that adjustment costs fall almost entirely on producers; and that the global value chain allocates value asymmetrically between the producing South and the consuming North. The paper finds all four propositions supported, though with different mechanism weights: fundamentals set the direction of price moves, financial structure sets their amplitude and tempo, demand rigidity determines who bears the cost, and value-chain governance determines who captures the gains.
papers.keywords: coffee price · commodity volatility · financialization · price elasticity of demand · North–South inequality

papers.title: The Making of a New "Taste of Yunnan": Quality Construction and Industrial Reorganization of Coffee as a Development Project
papers.affiliation: Professor of Sociology, School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University
papers.abstract: In recent years, Yunnan coffee has rapidly moved to the forefront of local development agendas, acquiring multiple meanings in relation to rural revitalization, high-quality development, and place-brand building. The rise of the coffee industry has not been driven solely by market expansion. Rather, against the backdrop of mature industries—most notably Pu’er tea—long occupying a central position in Yunnan’s regional economy, coffee has been constituted as a new object of development through the localization of the concept of “specialty coffee,” the formation of a shared understanding of quality, and the sustained organizational efforts of local governments. The development of the coffee industry does not represent the replacement of the established tea industry. Instead, it constitutes the cultivation of a new source of growth on the basis of existing governance experience and forms part of an ongoing process of recomposing the “Taste of Yunnan.” This process also reveals a distinctive generative logic of Chinese-style development projects: rather than starting from scratch, new economic growth is generated through linkages with established industries; rather than being passively incorporated into global industries, local actors become active agents in reshaping the global industrial landscape through local translation, combinatory forms of governance, and regional coordination.

papers.title: Transforming coffee landscapes in Lam Dong province, Viet Nam: from production expansion to intensification and quality-oriented development over a decade from 2014-2024
papers.abstract:
Lam Dong accounts for over 45.7% of Vietnam’s total coffee-growing area and is the country’s largest coffee-producing province. Over the past decade, its coffee landscapes have undergone a significant transformation from expansion-oriented production toward intensive, quality-oriented and more sustainable farming. This transformation extends beyond change in the cultivated areas to encompassed production systems, varieties, farmer organization, certification and market orientation.
Using the secondary data from 2014-2024, this study examines coffee development in the area corresponding to the former Lam Dong province, while considering its position within the newly established Lam Dong province following the 2025 provincial merger of the former Lam Dong, Dak Nong and Binh Thuan provinces.
The findings indicate that coffee development has increasingly relied on intensification rather than land expansion. The coffee –growing area increased by only 7.9% from 304. 6 thousand hectares in 2014 to 328.6 thousands hectares in 2024, while productivity increased 43.5% from 2.3 tons/ha to 3.3 tons, respectively. Coffee varieties have also diversified from predominantly Catimor toward high-yield varieties such as TR4, TR11, TRS1, and TS5 supported by government policies.
Meanwhile the coffee value chain has become more organized and quality-oriented. In 2014, only 12 enterprises were involved in the Lam Dong’s coffee industry.  Ten years later, 117 cooperatives, 32 farmer groups and 34 enterprises were collaborating with 28.949 coffee householders across the province. Certification schemes including Rainforest Alliance, UTZ, Vietgap and organic certifications together with 21 branding labels for coffee specialties, and geographical indications have expanded. International development organizations including RECOFTC, SNV and UNDP have further supported sustainable supply chain and landscape approaches.
The study argues that Lam Dong’s coffee landscape is being reshaped through the combined processes of intensification, diversification, value-chain upgrading, and sustainability – oriented interventions. This case provides insights into the broader transformation of smallholder coffee landscapes in Southeast Asia.
papers.keywords: coffee growers · livelihood · sustainable development

papers.title: Transforming the Coffee Value Chain: Strengthening producers for Quality and Sustainability
papers.coAuthors: Amorn Owatworakit, Sitthi Duangpet, Kitiphong Khongphinitbunjonga, Chalida Thaninkullaporn
papers.abstract: Arabica coffee producers have long been trapped in a cycle of low market prices driven by batch-to-batch quality inconsistencies and a limited understanding of global standards. To address these challenges, this study examined the transformation of coffee producers within the coffee value chain through the integration of scientific practices and standard. We demonstrate systematic change from the eleven coffee producers in Chiang Rai by implementing a standardized with  four-step scientific protocols; (1) a quality of cherry picking and testing, (2) pH-guided during fermentation (pH 4.0–4.5), (3) precision drying and monotoring, and (4) SCA-standard coffee green bean grading. Through cupping evaluations, interviews, and field visits following targeted workshops and training, we observed significant quality improvements. the cupping scores increased from 78 to 84 points, though one coffee producer showed no improvement and remained at 70 points. Furthermore, processing defect rates were reduced by approximately 20%. Notably, an increased proportion of lots scoring 75–84 points achieved a 20–25% price increase, while six producers utilizing natural and honey processes earned 20–40% premiums over washed lots. These results demonstrated that establishing measurable step controls through collaborative farmer-researcher-buyer knowledge enables quality reproducibility, offering a scalable model for extension services and graded purchasing programs.
papers.keywords: Arabica coffee · coffee value chain · coffee producers · quality standards
